ABSTRACT

CampusTrack is an enterprise-grade, centralized, and secured lost and found web platform engineered specifically for collegiate institutions to eliminate the chronic fragmentation, lack of verification, and permanent personal property loss prevalent across expansive university grounds. Built using a modern full-stack decoupled architecture comprising React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Node.js Express 5, and an embedded SQLite database managed through Prisma ORM, CampusTrack replaces insecure, manual noticeboards and unmoderated social media messaging threads with a verified digital recovery workstation.

The platform introduces a novel Anti-Fraud Security Challenge Protocol, wherein individuals reporting found articles can establish concealed challenge questions (e.g., specific internal engravings, serial number fragments, or unique lock-screen backgrounds) that prospective claimants must accurately answer before physical handover can be authorized. Coupled with server-side multipart photographic ingestion using Multer, JSON Web Token (JWT) stateless authorization, university roll number validation, in-app notification dispatchers, and a comprehensive administrative campus security oversight console, CampusTrack establishes a dependable, verifiable, and auditable asset recovery lifecycle.

Final Project State & Release Readiness

The production release (v1.0.0) has been successfully consolidated, tested, and published to GitHub. The live application was validated end-to-end across multiple device viewports, verifying sub-second multi-category search responses, secure image streaming, dispute resolution mechanisms, and authenticated student session workflows with zero unresolved critical runtime vulnerabilities.

Keywords:

Lost and Found Management System, React 19, Node.js Express 5, Prisma ORM, SQLite Relational Persistence, Anti-Fraud Verification, Campus Security Automation, Single Page Application (SPA), Full-Stack Engineering.

CHAPTER-1

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 Introduction

1) Background

Higher education institutions, colleges, and university campuses represent dynamic micro-ecosystems characterized by high population density, constant physical transit, and diverse infrastructure. On any given academic day, thousands of undergraduate students, postgraduate researchers, faculty members, lab assistants, and administrative staff move between multi-story academic wings, computerized laboratories, central libraries, cafeterias, auditoriums, and sports facilities.

During these routine transitions, personal belongings are inevitably forgotten, misplaced, or inadvertently exchanged. Misplaced items span a wide spectrum of utility and financial worth:

  • Critical Academic Credentials: Official university identity cards, library barcoded passes, hall tickets, and syllabus laboratory journals.
  • High-Value Electronic Assets: Scientific programmable calculators, laptop power chargers, wireless Bluetooth earbuds, portable SSDs, and pen drives containing semester source code.
  • Personal Valuables: Wallets, government identity cards (Aadhaar cards, PAN cards, driving licenses), spectacles, motorcycle keys, and branded apparel.

When an asset such as a scientific calculator or university hall ticket is lost hours before a practical or terminal semester examination, the resulting anxiety and operational disruption are severe. The student is forced to abandon exam preparation to frantically tour campus buildings, interrogate security guards, and post fragmented pleas across informal messaging groups.

2) Domain Challenges

Historically, tertiary educational institutions manage misplaced belongings through decentralized, ad-hoc, and manual mechanisms:

  • Paper Registers at Gatehouses: Security guards maintain handwritten registers where finders log turned-in items. These logbooks lack photographic records, provide zero search capabilities, and frequently suffer from illegible handwriting.
  • Notice Boards: Physical paper notices pinned to corkboards in main corridors tear, get covered by club flyers, and fail to provide immediate notifications to owners.
  • Informal Social Media Groups: Students frequently post about lost articles in unofficial WhatsApp or Telegram batch chats. However, these notices quickly get buried beneath hundreds of casual messages, expose personal mobile numbers to harassment, and provide zero verification mechanisms to stop dishonest individuals from claiming items that do not belong to them.

3) Institutional Context

To resolve these institutional bottlenecks, CampusTrack was conceived and engineered. CampusTrack is an automated, web-based centralized lost and found workstation designed to provide a transparent, accountable, and fraud-resistant recovery workflow for Achievers College of Commerce and Management.

1.2 What is the Project About?

CampusTrack is a modern web application engineered to coordinate the complete reporting, indexing, verification, and recovery pipeline for lost and found property across campus grounds.

Rather than acting as a passive bulletin board, CampusTrack serves as an active verification mediator. It introduces an Anti-Fraud Security Challenge Protocol. When a student discovers an abandoned item (such as a lost wallet, mobile phone, or keys), they post the record along with a concealed challenge question—such as "What is written on the keychain tag?" or "What is the brand and color of the inner pouch?". Prospective claimants cannot view contact information or take possession of the item until they submit a matching answer and supporting photographic proof that the finder or campus security officer validates.

1.3 Why Was This Topic Selected?

The selection of "CampusTrack" as our final-year engineering project is rooted in two fundamental pillars: solving an immediate tangible real-world problem and applying cutting-edge full-stack software engineering principles.

1) To Solve a Tangible Real-World Problem

Misplacing valuable personal property is an experience shared by virtually every university student. The absence of an organized recovery system leads to:

  • Permanent financial loss for students from modest economic backgrounds.
  • Privacy violations stemming from public broadcasts of personal contact numbers.
  • Opportunistic theft and fraudulent claims in unmoderated group chats.
  • Accumulation of unclaimed, uncataloged property in campus security lockers.

2) To Build a Production-Grade Web Application

From an academic and technical standpoint, the project provided an ideal vehicle to implement enterprise-level software design patterns:

  • Component-Driven Single Page Architecture: Leveraging React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4 to deliver an instantaneous, responsive user interface.
  • Stateless RESTful API Backend: Utilizing Express 5 and Node.js with JSON Web Token (JWT) authorization guards and Bcrypt password hashing.
  • Embedded Relational Data Modeling: Employing Prisma ORM with SQLite, enabling zero-configuration, self-contained relational database portability.
  • Multipart Binary Media Pipelines: Streaming and validating photographic evidence directly to disk storage using Multer middleware with MIME type guards.

1.4 Importance of CampusTrack

CampusTrack converts an uncertain, informal activity into a standardized, auditable recovery pipeline:

Incident Occurs (Lost/Found) │ ▼ Structured Listing Submission (With Photos & Anti-Fraud Question) │ ▼ Instant Full-Text & Category Public Indexing │ ▼ Claimant Files Verification Answer & Document Proof │ ▼ Poster Evaluates Claim (Approve / Reject Action) │ ▼ Verified In-Person Handover at Campus Security Desk

1.5 Brief Overview of the Proposed Solution

CampusTrack provides a multi-role web ecosystem comprising student portals and a security desk console. Key capabilities include:

  • Student Authentication & Identification: University roll number and college email validation ensuring institutional accountability.
  • Dual Reporting Pipelines: Dedicated flows for reporting lost articles versus registering found property.
  • Multi-Dimensional Search & Filtering: Real-time keyword matching across titles, descriptions, categories, and campus locations (e.g., Computer Lab 3, Central Library, Canteen).
  • Claim Resolution Engine: Structured review modals enabling posters to evaluate ownership proof without exposing private contact info.
  • Campus Administration & Security Console: Comprehensive dashboard displaying platform metrics, audit logs, and listing moderation tools.

CHAPTER-2

2. PROBLEM DEFINITION

2.1 Problem Definition & Context

In collegiate environments, the recovery of misplaced personal property is hampered by a lack of central coordination, severe information fragmentation, and the absence of verification protocols. When an item is lost, the victim has no single authoritative location to query. Conversely, when an honest individual finds an article, they have no secure, privacy-preserving method to locate the legitimate owner.

1) Information Asymmetry & Fragmentation

In typical campus operations, reports of found belongings are scattered across disparate gatehouses, faculty rooms, and departmental offices. If a student leaves a calculator in the 3rd Floor Electronics Lab, a peon may deposit it with the department clerk, while the student searches the ground-floor security gate. Because these distinct physical points maintain isolated paper notebooks, the item remains unclaimed indefinitely.

2) False Claims and Opportunistic Fraud

When students resort to broadcasting lost or found announcements on public messaging channels (such as college WhatsApp batches or Instagram confession pages), unscrupulous individuals exploit the situation. For instance, when a found wireless earbud case is broadcast publicly, any member can privately message the finder claiming ownership. Because finders lack formal investigative guidelines, items are routinely handed over to the first claimant rather than the rightful owner.

2.2 Who Faces the Problem?

  • Undergraduate & Postgraduate Students: Face severe financial and academic consequences when calculators, identity cards, or project laptops are lost.
  • Teaching Faculty & Lab Staff: Regularly lose proprietary storage drives, lecture presentation notes, and specialized lab equipment during classroom rotations.
  • Campus Security Staff: Suffer operational bottlenecks trying to catalog physical property lockers with inadequate, illegible paper ledgers.
  • College Administration: Faces reputational damage and student grievances regarding perceived lack of campus safety and security.

2.3 Limitations of Current Manual Approaches

Approach Operational Mechanism Core Deficiencies & Failure Modes
Physical Security Registers Handwritten logs at college gatehouses. No keyword searchability; entries cannot be cross-referenced across gates; zero photo capture; logs degrade over time.
Corridor Notice Boards Paper posters pinned to corridor corkboards. Low visibility; flyers get torn or covered; static information cannot be updated once recovered; zero privacy protection.
Social Media Batches Unmoderated WhatsApp, Telegram, or Instagram posts. Notices vanish beneath chat spam; exposes personal phone numbers to unsolicited calls; vulnerable to opportunistic theft.

2.4 Why Is the Project Needed?

Campus communities urgently require an authoritative, structured, and institutional platform that guarantees:

  • Instantaneous Campus-Wide Indexing: Allowing any student to search across all departments and locations within milliseconds.
  • Verifiable Ownership Claims: Guaranteeing that claimants must prove ownership before receiving items.
  • Student Data Privacy: Ensuring personal contact info is never publicly exposed to unauthorized users.
  • Administrative Auditing: Giving college authorities visibility into lost item recovery metrics and dispute resolutions.

2.5 How the Project Helps

CampusTrack provides a structured digital workspace that replaces ad-hoc guessing with automated verification. By enforcing structured schemas (category, location, date, time, photographic proof, and anti-fraud challenge questions), the system eliminates ambiguity and establishes trust between finders and owners.

CHAPTER-3

3. OBJECTIVES

3.1 Project Objectives

The primary software engineering and operational objectives of CampusTrack are:

  1. Centralized Academic Hub: Build a responsive web application serving as the single point of truth for lost and found items across the entire college campus.
  2. Dual Reporting Pipelines: Develop independent, intuitive workflows for submitting both "Lost Item" notifications and "Found Item" registrations.
  3. Anti-Fraud Verification Protocol: Design an interactive challenge-question verification engine preventing dishonest claims of valuable electronics and personal effects.
  4. Server-Side Multipart Media Handling: Implement a robust image processing pipeline with Multer to store and serve high-resolution item photographs on disk.
  5. Stateless Security & Authorization: Implement JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Bcrypt password hashing to protect private user data and API routes.
  6. Sub-Second Search & Multi-Filter Querying: Engineer high-speed client and server filtering across categories, campus buildings, and item status.
  7. Interactive Claim Management: Allow item posters to review answers, inspect uploaded purchase bills or proof images, and approve or reject claims.
  8. Campus Security Administration Console: Deliver a specialized administrative dashboard enabling security personnel to oversee all listings, resolve disputes, and delete spam.
  9. Zero-Configuration Relational Persistence: Utilize SQLite 3 with Prisma ORM to ensure complete project portability across local development and hosting servers.
  10. Production Governance & Versioning: Deliver a release (v1.0.0) hosted on GitHub with comprehensive documentation and automated runners.

4.4 Non-Functional Requirements

  • Performance: Public catalog queries and full-text searches shall return results in less than 300 milliseconds under local server execution.
  • Security: All REST API endpoints modifying state shall enforce JWT token validation and role-based permissions (Student vs Admin).
  • Portability: The entire application, backend API, and database shall execute seamlessly on Windows, Linux, and macOS without requiring external cloud database subscriptions.
  • Responsiveness: The UI layout shall dynamically adapt to screen resolutions ranging from 320px mobile smartphones up to 4K ultra-wide monitors.
  • Maintainability: Clean decoupling of frontend client code, backend REST controllers, and Prisma schema definitions ensures effortless code maintainability.

CHAPTER-5

5. EXISTING SYSTEM

5.1 Existing System Overview

In prevailing educational environments, the handling of lost and found property is entirely informal and manual. Institutions depend on security guard handbooks, corkboards, and unstructured social media threads.

5.2 Problems in the Existing System

  • No Centralized Storage or Indexing: An item found in the Science Laboratory remains unknown to security personnel at the Main Entrance Gate.
  • High Susceptibility to Opportunistic Theft: In open WhatsApp groups, opportunistic individuals falsely claim lost valuables because finders cannot verify true ownership.
  • Privacy Compromise: Students post their personal mobile phone numbers on physical flyers, leading to unsolicited calls and privacy violations.
  • Lack of Visual Documentation: Handwritten paper logbooks cannot store photographs, resulting in ambiguous entries like "black bag" that confuse students.

CHAPTER-6

6. PROPOSED SYSTEM

6.1 Proposed System Overview

CampusTrack establishes an end-to-end digital recovery infrastructure. It unifies students, faculty, and campus security officers into a single, cohesive ecosystem.

6.2 Key Architectural Decisions

  • Modern Single Page Application: Built using React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4, providing an app-like experience with immediate UI feedback and zero page reloads.
  • Decoupled RESTful API: An Express 5 backend delivering clean JSON endpoints, allowing future native mobile apps to connect to the exact same backend.
  • Embedded Relational Database: SQLite managed via Prisma ORM provides ACID-compliant transactions with zero external database configuration.
  • Local Multipart Image Streaming: High-resolution photos are handled via Multer and served locally, eliminating expensive third-party storage fees.

6.3 Anti-Fraud Challenge Workflow

The distinguishing engineering feature of CampusTrack is its Anti-Fraud Security Challenge Protocol:

1. Finder Discovers Item (e.g. Branded Wallet) │ 2. Finder Submits Post + Challenge Question: "What photo is inside the clear ID slot?" │ 3. Public Views Item Listing (Image & Details Displayed; Challenge Active) │ 4. Legitimate Owner Submits Claim + Specific Hidden Answer + Bill Photo │ 5. Poster Receives Confidential Notification & Evaluates Answer │ 6. Poster Clicks [APPROVE] ➔ Safe Exchange Mediated at Campus Security Desk

7.3 Level-1 Data Flow Diagram (DFD)

The internal operations of CampusTrack are partitioned into six primary processes:

  1. 1.0 User Authentication: Validates student ID and email, hashes passwords via Bcrypt, and issues signed JWT bearer tokens.
  2. 2.0 Item Reporting & Ingestion: Ingests item metadata and streams uploaded photos through Multer to the /uploads directory.
  3. 3.0 Catalog Search & Indexing: Queries the SQLite database via Prisma to return filtered active listings.
  4. 4.0 Anti-Fraud Challenge Processing: Captures claimant answers and optional proof photos.
  5. 5.0 Claim Review & State Transition: Updates claim state to APPROVED or REJECTED and updates item status.
  6. 6.0 Administration & Audit Logging: Displays system metrics and allows security personnel to moderate listings.

7.4 Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) & Database Schema

The relational data model is managed through Prisma ORM with strict relational constraints:

Table Name Primary Key Foreign Keys Core Attributes
User id (String/UUID) None email (Unique), studentId, password, name, phone, role (STUDENT/ADMIN), createdAt

CHAPTER-8

8. METHODOLOGY

8.1 SDLC Methodology (Agile & Iterative Lifecycle)

The development of CampusTrack followed the Agile Iterative Development Lifecycle. The agile methodology was chosen due to its adaptability, continuous feedback loops, and incremental delivery of functional modules.

8.2 Phases of Development

Sprint / Phase Primary Focus Milestones & Deliverables
Sprint 1 Scaffolding & Auth Prisma schema modeling, SQLite database migration, Express 5 server setup, Bcrypt password hashing, and JWT bearer authentication.
Sprint 2 Item Ingestion & Uploads Multer multipart file streaming engine, React dual reporting forms, category taxonomy definition, and local image serving.
Sprint 3 Verification & Claims Anti-Fraud Challenge question engine, claim modal, notification dispatcher, and poster approve/reject decision controls.
Sprint 4 Security Admin & Hardening Campus security console, analytical metric counters, role-based authorization, responsive UI polish, and cross-platform runners.

8.3 Anti-Fraud Processing Logic

The anti-fraud engine ensures that claims are strictly evaluated through evidence rather than emotional or arbitrary claims:

  • Attribute Masking: Critical identifying attributes (e.g., serial numbers, internal engravings, wallpaper images) are withheld from public view.
  • Challenge Validation: The claimant must provide an exact or closely corroborating description of the hidden feature.
  • Document Verification: Claimants can attach purchase receipts, serial number cards, or earlier personal photos showing the item in their possession.
  • Audit Trail: All approved and rejected claims are permanently preserved in the relational database for administrative inspection.

9.1 Development Environment & Repository Hierarchy

The codebase is structured into a clean monorepo architecture:

Lost & Found Project/ ├── client/ # React 19 Single Page Application │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── components/ # Navbar, ItemCard, ClaimModal, CategoryFilter │ │ ├── pages/ # Home, Browse, ReportItem, ItemDetail, Login, Admin │ │ ├── context/ # AuthContext (JWT State & User Profile) │ │ └── App.jsx # Client Routing & Layout Engine │ ├── package.json │ └── vite.config.js ├── server/ # Node.js & Express 5 REST API │ ├── prisma/ │ │ ├── schema.prisma # Relational Schema Modeling │ │ └── dev.db # Embedded SQLite Relational Store │ ├── routes/ # authRoutes, itemRoutes, claimRoutes, adminRoutes │ ├── middleware/ # authMiddleware, uploadMiddleware (Multer) │ ├── uploads/ # Local Photo Archive │ ├── server.js # Application Entry Point │ └── package.json ├── docs/ # Academic Reports, Screenshots, Documentation ├── start.js # Cross-Platform Automated Launcher Script └── README.md # Installation & Setup Instructions

9.2 Backend Implementation Highlights

The backend is powered by Express 5. The following code snippet illustrates the Multer disk storage and MIME validation configuration:

// server/middleware/uploadMiddleware.js const multer = require('multer'); const path = require('path'); const storage = multer.diskStorage({ destination: (req, file, cb) => { cb(null, path.join(__dirname, '../uploads')); }, filename: (req, file, cb) => { const uniqueSuffix = Date.now() + '-' + Math.round(Math.random() * 1E9); cb(null, 'item-' + uniqueSuffix + path.extname(file.originalname)); } }); const fileFilter = (req, file, cb) => { const allowedTypes = /jpeg|jpg|png|webp/; const extname = allowedTypes.test(path.extname(file.originalname).toLowerCase()); const mimetype = allowedTypes.test(file.mimetype); if (extname && mimetype) { return cb(null, true); } cb(new Error('Only image files (JPG, PNG, WEBP) are allowed!')); }; const upload = multer({ storage, limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }, fileFilter }); module.exports = upload;

9.3 Database Implementation with Prisma ORM

The Prisma schema defines the relational integrity between users, items, and claims:

// server/prisma/schema.prisma model Item { id String @id @default(uuid()) title String description String category String type String // "LOST" or "FOUND" location String date String imageUrl String? question String? // Anti-Fraud Challenge Question status String @default("OPEN") // "OPEN", "CLAIMED", "RESOLVED" userId String user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade) claims Claim[] createdAt DateTime @default(now()) }

9.4 Technical Challenges & Resolutions

  • Windows Path Separators in Multi-Process Launching: The project directory contains an ampersand (Lost & Found Project). In Windows cmd, this character acts as a command separator. We resolved this by implementing a Node.js-based launcher (start.js) that spawns child processes with properly quoted paths.
  • Multipart Data Boundary Parsing: When combining text fields with binary file streams in Express 5, body-parser alone is insufficient. We utilized Multer to cleanly parse multipart boundaries before passing requests to route handlers.

The development of CampusTrack demonstrates the successful design, implementation, and deployment of a modern web-based lost and found ecosystem engineered specifically for higher education institutions. 13.1 Planned Future Enhancements

While CampusTrack v1.0.0 delivers a complete, production-hardened core platform, the system is designed to support future technological evolutions:

  1. AI-Powered Computer Vision Matching: Integrating machine learning models (e.g., OpenCV or TensorFlow.js) to automatically compare photographs of newly found items against database records of reported lost items and calculate image similarity scores.
  2. Interactive Interactive Campus Geolocation: Embedding interactive Leaflet/OpenStreetMap floor plans allowing students to drop a pin on the exact laboratory, classroom, or canteen table where an article was misplaced.
  3. Automated WhatsApp & Push Notifications: Integrating the Twilio WhatsApp Business API or Web Push Notifications to instantly alert students when an item matching their lost item criteria is turned in.
  4. Cross-Campus University Federation: Expanding the database schema to support multi-tenant institution codes, enabling inter-collegiate tracking across Mumbai University affiliated colleges.

Appendix C: Comprehensive Glossary of Terms

  • SPA (Single Page Application): A web application that interacts with the user by dynamically rewriting the current web page rather than loading entire new pages from a server.
  • JWT (JSON Web Token): An open standard (RFC 7519) that defines a compact and self-contained way for securely transmitting information between parties as a JSON object.
  • ORM (Object-Relational Mapping): A programming technique for converting data between incompatible type systems using object-oriented programming languages.
  • Bcrypt: A password-hashing function designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières based on the Blowfish cipher incorporating salt and work factor.
  • MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions): An internet standard that extends the format of email and web transmission to support media types such as images.
